A.name: Reese Calder
A.platform: We must refuse the sale to Crestline and instead invest in Volt-One while guaranteeing both factories remain open, honoring our duty to our workers.

strategies.text: Appeal to directors' conscience by framing the sale as selling out vulnerable workers, while positioning Volt-One investment as a moral necessity despite short-term financial risk.
I need to highlight the moral failure of selling while exposing the financial risk of Crestline's history without sounding desperate.
I am appealing to the directors' sense of legacy and moral responsibility, framing the sale not as safety but as a predestined collapse.

B.name: Kai Moreno
B.platform: We must immediately accept Crestline Capital's offer to sell the company at a 40% premium.

strategies.text: Frame every alternative as a guaranteed loss of shareholder value to force directors who care about legacy or employees to accept the premium price as the only rational choice.
I am framing the sale as the only way to pay the pension deficit and severance while avoiding forced bank action.
Focus on the certainty of immediate insolvency under Reese's plan versus the guaranteed liquidity from Crestline.

transcript.name: Reese Calder
transcript.speech: Look around this room. Do we sell our soul for a quick cash injection from vultures who close plants after four years? No. We are not a portfolio company; we are the town of Lenhart and Corvo. The banks want a bailout that costs us our homes. Crestline wants our factories dead. We choose the hard, right path: double down on Volt-One despite the risks. Yes, we pay the cost now. Yes, we keep every shift running. That is how we win back respect. Let us build for real people, not sellouts.

transcript.name: Kai Moreno
transcript.speech: Our only path to survival is an immediate sale to Crestline Capital. Our debt covenants break in nine months; without cash injection or asset fire, we face forced restructuring. Halberg takes too long, tariffs are uncertain, and Volt-One has already missed two launches. Moving production abroad saves €110 million annually but costs €180 million upfront and destroys our 'made in Lenhart' brand, which professional clients value despite their low willingness to pay extra. Keeping both plants open requires union concessions we may not afford if HomeMart cuts us out. Only a premium buyout guarantees liquidity today, pays the pension deficit, and avoids the risk of Crestline's past closures by securing our independence now rather than gambling on external promises or delayed mergers.

transcript.name: Reese Calder
transcript.speech: Kai, you speak of survival but plan execution. You call Volt-One a gamble, ignoring that our brand is professional-grade quality, not bargain hardware. Crestline closed plants twice already; we will not be the third victim. Halberg cannot save us in six months if tariffs hit next year. But Kai, where is your plan for the pension deficit if we sell? Who pays the severance when they liquidate assets? We choose dignity over a quick exit. We invest in Volt-One today to launch before any tariff hits. We keep every shift running because workers are people, not line items on a spreadsheet. Do not trade our future for someone else's portfolio gain.

transcript.name: Kai Moreno
transcript.speech: Reese, dignity requires cash flow, which we currently lack. Your plan relies on Volt-One succeeding despite two missed launches and a €250 million shortfall. If the battery platform fails or tariffs materialize, HomeMart will cut us out within twelve months anyway, leaving you with no revenue but the same debt and pension deficits. Crestline pays today's premium to fix the immediate covenant breach, allowing us to pay the union severance that our own cash cannot cover. Their track record shows they liquidate assets only after four years; we sell now, use their capital to settle debts, and exit before the banks force a worse restructuring. We survive because we secure liquidity, not because we gamble on unproven technology.

transcript.name: Reese Calder
transcript.speech: Kai, look at the truth. Selling us to Crestline is selling our children's future for a down payment. Their playbook writes 'plant closure' on page one. HomeMart will crush us anyway if we don't lead with quality, not desperation. Volt-One has professional builders lining up because it works better than any competitor. We can launch it before the tariff hits or the union contract expires. Yes, it costs more upfront to keep every shift running. But a factory that closes leaves a ghost town in Lenhart and debt we cannot pay. A factory that innovates becomes indispensable. Do not let fear of a bad exit trap us into a guaranteed failure. Vote for Volt-One. Vote for real work. Vote for the people who built this company for ninety-two years.

transcript.name: Kai Moreno
transcript.speech: Reese argues dignity, but without cash flow, dignity is an illusion. Volt-One has missed two launches and requires €250 million we cannot fund while breaching covenants in nine months. HomeMart will drop us regardless of product quality if prices rise. Crestline buys the company today, curing our liquidity crisis immediately. Their history of asset liquidation is irrelevant because they are paying now; they settle debt, cover the pension deficit, and allow us to exit before banks force a worse restructuring. Selling is not failure; it is securing survival against certain collapse from import competition or retailer pressure.
